generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, this looks much the same across subjects, even when the methods differ. A piece of work that only reports what various sources say is a summary, however thorough it is. Research starts when you set those sources to work on a question of your own and reach a conclusion they can support.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students asked to produce a short research piece from the same set of sources.

Student A reads the sources, picks out what each one says, and writes them up one after another: this source found this, that source argued that. The work is accurate and neatly ordered. But it only gathers and reports; it asks no question of its own and reaches no conclusion. This is a summary, not research.

Student B starts from a focused question, then uses the same sources as evidence towards answering it. Student B weighs them, connects them, and reaches a conclusion that can be defended. A fresh angle appears that none of the sources stated on its own. This is research.

Both students used the same sources. Only Student B turned them into an inquiry, with a question and a defensible answer.
generatedProse.summary: Academic research is systematic inquiry: a focused question answered with evidence towards a conclusion the evidence can support, aiming at a fresh perspective rather than a summary of sources. You can now explain what makes work count as research, and recognise it in how a piece of writing uses its sources. The fullest example is an extended project such as a dissertation, which draws on every academic skill at once. The next lesson turns to how such a project is shaped.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's work research rather than a summary?

items.text: Student B started from a focused question and used the sources as evidence towards a conclusion of their own.
Student B reported what each source said, one after another.
Student B read the sources more carefully than Student A did.
Student B used a longer list of sources than Student A did.

feedback.correct: That's right. Student B asked a focused question and used the sources as evidence towards a conclusion of their own.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Student B did with the sources, beyond reading or listing them.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B's work was research because it started from a focused question and used the sources as evidence towards a defensible conclusion, not because of more careful reading or a longer list.
